1                                 NOTICE OF MOTION AND MOTION

2    TO ALL PARTIES HEREIN AND THEIR ATTORNEYS OF RECORD:
3             PLEASE TAKE NOTICE that on ______________, 2026, or as soon thereafter as the

4    matter may be heard, Plaintiff Ex-Human Inc. (“Ex-Human”) will and hereby does move this Court,

5    pursuant to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65 and Civil Local Rule 65-1, for a Temporary

6    Restraining Order and an Order to Show Cause Why a Preliminary Injunction Should Not Issue

7    requiring Defendant Apple Inc. and its officers, employees, agents, and all persons acting in concert

8    with them (collectively, “Apple”) to reinstate Ex-Human’s Apple Developer Program membership
9    and developer account, restore Ex-Human’s iOS applications to the App Store, and to cease

10   withholding earnings associated with Ex-Human’s developer account, pending further order of this

11   Court.

12            This motion is based on Apple’s termination of Ex-Human’s developer account on March

13   13, 2026, after invoking misconduct-based provisions of the Apple Developer Program License

14   Agreement, including Section 3.2(f), while failing to identify the conduct it contends justified that
15   determination, and its continued enforcement of that termination on the same basis.

16            This motion is made on the grounds that: (1) absent immediate relief, Ex-Human will suffer

17   irreparable harm from continued exclusion from the iOS platform; (2) Ex-Human is likely to
18   succeed on the merits or at minimum raises serious questions as to whether Apple may continue to

19   enforce termination on a misconduct-based rationale without identifying the conduct it contends

20   violated the parties’ agreement; (3) the balance of equities tips sharply in Ex-Human’s favor

21   because Apple has identified no concrete harm that would result from temporary reinstatement; and

22   (4) the public interest supports interim relief.

23            This motion is based upon the Complaint in this action (Dkt. 1), this Notice of Motion, the
24   accompanying Memorandum of Points and Authorities, the Declaration of Artem Rodichev, the

25   proposed Temporary Restraining Order and Order to Show Cause, all matters subject to judicial

26   notice, and such further evidence as may be presented.

1                                            INTRODUCTION
2           Ex-Human seeks a temporary restraining order restoring its Apple Developer Program

3    account and reinstating its iOS applications. Apple terminated Ex-Human’s account after accusing

4    it of “dishonest or fraudulent activity” under Section 3.2(f), but never identified the conduct that

5    supposedly justified that determination. Across multiple notices and appeals, Apple relied on

6    generalized, boilerplate descriptions of possible misconduct while continuing to enforce complete

7    exclusion from the iOS platform.

8           That ongoing exclusion is causing immediate and irreparable harm. Ex-Human has lost

9    access to its iOS user base, its subscription relationships have been disrupted, and its position in a

10   fast-moving consumer market is deteriorating in ways that cannot be fully repaired through

11   damages. Because the App Store is the only authorized distribution channel for native iOS

12   applications, Ex-Human cannot reach those users through any alternative channel.

13          Ex-Human is likely to succeed on the merits because Apple continues to enforce termination

14   on a misconduct-based rationale while refusing to identify the conduct it contends triggered that

15   determination. At minimum, this raises serious questions under the implied covenant of good faith

16   and fair dealing. Interim relief would preserve the status quo that existed before Apple’s January

17   24, 2026 actions, and Apple has identified no concrete risk that would result from temporary

18   reinstatement pending adjudication on the merits.

19                                      FACTUAL BACKGROUND
20          A.      Apple’s App Store and Developer Program
21          Apple operates the App Store as the only authorized distribution channel for native iOS
22   applications on iPhone in the United States. Complaint (“Compl.”) ¶¶ 20, 66. Developers must
23   participate in Apple’s Developer Program and comply with the Apple Developer Program License
24   Agreement (“DPLA”) to distribute applications to iOS users. Id. at ¶¶ 20-22.
25          Under that framework, Apple controls both initial access to the App Store and the continued
26   availability of applications through its review and enforcement processes. Id. at ¶¶ 20, 22-23. Apple
27   also processes in-app purchases and subscriptions through its payment system and collects and
28   remits developer proceeds pursuant to Schedule 2 of the DPLA. Id. at ¶¶ 24, 60, 62.
                                          1
                          MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
       Case 3:26-cv-02798-JD          Document 23        Filed 04/22/26      Page 6 of 19



1            Section 3.2(f) of the DPLA prohibits “dishonest or fraudulent activity” in connection with

2    a developer’s applications. Compl. ¶ 42. Apple invoked that provision as the basis for the actions
3    at issue here. Id.

4            B.      Ex-Human and Its Applications
5            Ex-Human develops consumer-facing artificial intelligence applications, including Botify

6    AI (“Botify”) and Photify AI (“Photify”). Id. at ¶ 31. Over the past five years, Ex-Human has built

7    its technology, products, and user base through more than $10 million in investment, including $4

8    million in venture capital funding. Declaration of Artem Rodichev (“Rodichev Decl.”) ¶ 2.
9            Botify, launched in 2021, had remained continuously available on the App Store for nearly

10   four years, accumulated more than 2.3 million iOS installs, and generated approximately $330,000

11   in monthly revenue prior to its removal. Compl. ¶ 34. Photify, launched in 2024, generated

12   approximately $100,000 in monthly revenue before it was removed from the App Store. Id. at ¶ 35.

13           Ex-Human’s ability to distribute these applications, maintain subscription-based

14   relationships with users, and operate its iOS business depends on continued access to its Apple
15   Developer Program account and the App Store. Id. at ¶ 32.
16           C.      Apple’s Misconduct Allegations and Termination Without Identified Conduct
17           On January 24, 2026, Apple issued a “Pending Termination Notice” asserting that Ex-
18   Human’s developer account had been used for “dishonest or fraudulent activity” under Section

19   3.2(f) of the DPLA. Id. at ¶ 42. Apple simultaneously removed Photify from the App Store and

20   froze all earnings payments. Id. Ex-Human did not understand why it received that notice. Ex-

21   Human had not engaged in dishonest or fraudulent activity, and its repeated efforts in the weeks

22   that followed to obtain clarification from Apple yielded no meaningful explanation. Rodichev Decl.

23   ¶ 14.
24           Apple’s notice did not identify any specific submission, transaction, content item, or other

25   act that purportedly violated Section 3.2(f). Compl. ¶¶ 42-43. It referred generally to prior guideline

26   violations but did not identify the correspondence or conduct at issue. Id. at ¶ 43. Ex-Human

27   promptly submitted an appeal providing detailed information about its applications, including their

28

1    technical architecture and content-moderation systems, and offering to implement any additional

2    safeguards Apple required. Id. at ¶ 44.
3           On February 10, 2026, Apple denied the appeal, stating that it had identified a “pattern of

4    manipulative or misleading behavior” and listing categories of possible violations, including

5    inaccurate metadata, misleading content, and ratings manipulation. Id. at ¶ 45. Apple did not state

6    which, if any, of those categories it attributed to Ex-Human and did not identify any specific

7    submission, transaction, or act. Compl. ¶ 45.

8           Ex-Human submitted a reinstatement petition on February 11, 2026, and additional appeals
9    thereafter, repeatedly attempting to address Apple’s concerns and offering to implement further

10   safeguards. Id. at ¶ 46.

11          Apple denied each appeal using substantially similar language. Id. at ¶¶ 45, 47-48, 50. It

12   continued to cite Section 3.2(f) and later referenced App Review Guidelines 1.1, 1.1.4, and 5.6, but

13   again did not identify any specific submission, transaction, content item, or act underlying its

14   determination. Id. Throughout this process, Ex-Human attempted to engage directly with Apple’s
15   App Review team, including through multiple requests for calls. Id. at ¶¶ 44, 46, 49, 52-53;

16   Rodichev Decl. ¶¶ 24-25. Those requests were denied. Rodichev Decl. ¶ 25. Following termination

17   of Ex-Human’s developer account, Ex-Human lost access to App Store Connect and the related
18   systems through which it had submitted appeals, petitions, and communicated with Apple’s App

19   Review and Business Management teams, leaving it with no remaining channel to communicate

20   with Apple. Id. at ¶ 30.

21          On March 13, 2026, Apple formally terminated Ex-Human’s developer account. Compl. ¶

22   54. The termination notice again asserted “fraudulent conduct” but did not identify any specific

23   factual basis for that determination. Id. As a result, Botify was removed from the App Store, iOS
24   payment processing ceased, and Ex-Human lost access to its iOS user base. Id. Across all

25   communications, Apple repeatedly accused Ex-Human of serious misconduct but did not identify

26   the conduct it contends violated Section 3.2(f) or the cited guidelines, while continuing to enforce

27   termination and exclusion from the platform. Id. at ¶¶ 45, 47-48, 50, 54.

1           D.      Apple’s Withholding of Earned Proceeds Without Accounting

2           Apple paused all earnings payments to Ex-Human effective January 24, 2026 and has

3    withheld approximately $506,000 in developer proceeds generated from completed App Store

4    transactions. Rodichev Decl. ¶ 31. Those funds were collected by Apple through its in-app payment

5    system in its role as Ex-Human’s agent for processing end-user transactions. Compl. ¶ 56. Apple

6    has access to transaction-level data sufficient to identify refunds, chargebacks, or other adjustments.

7    Compl. ¶ 57.

8           Apple has not identified any specific transaction that it contends is fraudulent, invalid, or

9    subject to chargeback. Id. at ¶ 57. It has not provided any accounting of the withheld funds or

10   identified any portion of those funds as tied to refunds or other offsets. Id. at ¶ 58. Based on Ex-

11   Human’s historical data, refund rates for its applications are low and would account for only a small

12   fraction of the approximately $506,000 withheld. Rodichev Decl. ¶ 35. Apple has not represented

13   that the withheld funds have been applied to any identified refund obligation or other transaction-

14   specific basis. Compl. ¶ 61.

15          E.      Ongoing Harm from Exclusion from the iOS Platform

16          Apple’s termination of Ex-Human’s developer account has eliminated Ex-Human’s ability

17   to distribute its applications to iOS users through the App Store, the only authorized distribution

18   channel for native iOS applications in the United States. Id. at ¶¶ 63, 66. As a result, Ex-Human

19   has lost access to its iOS user base, disrupted ongoing subscription relationships, and eliminated its

20   primary iOS revenue streams. Id. at ¶ 64; Rodichev Decl. ¶ 37-40. Users have contacted Ex-Human

21   regarding the unavailability of its applications and the inability to continue using or purchasing

22   services through iOS. Rodichev Decl. ¶ 39.

6                                               ARGUMENT
7             A temporary restraining order should issue because Ex-Human is suffering immediate and
8    irreparable harm, is likely to succeed on the merits or at least raises serious questions going to the
9    merits, the balance of equities tips sharply in its favor, and an injunction is in the public interest.
10   Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7, 20, 129 S. Ct. 365, 374, 172 L. Ed. 2d 249 (2008).
11   Under the Ninth Circuit’s sliding-scale approach, a strong showing on irreparable harm and the
12   balance of equities supports relief where serious questions exist on the merits. Alliance for the Wild
13   Rockies v. Cottrell, 632 F.3d 1127, 1134-35 (9th Cir. 2011).
14   I.       EX-HUMAN IS SUFFERING IMMEDIATE AND IRREPARABLE HARM
              ABSENT INTERIM RELIEF
15

16            Apple’s termination of Ex-Human’s developer account has already caused, and continues
17   to cause, irreparable harm. Ex-Human has been excluded from the iOS platform, lost access to its
18   iOS user base, and experienced disruption to ongoing subscription relationships and user
19   engagement that cannot be fully remedied through monetary damages. Compl. ¶¶ 64, 66. This is
20   not a case involving temporary lost revenue; it is a case involving ongoing exclusion from the only
21   channel through which Ex-Human can reach iOS users.
22            Loss of Access to the Only iOS Distribution Channel. The App Store is the only authorized
23   distribution channel for native iOS applications in the United States. Id. at ¶ 66. Without access to
24   its developer account, Ex-Human cannot distribute its applications to iOS users, maintain existing
25   user relationships through that channel, or restore its position in the iOS ecosystem. Id. Such
26   “[e]vidence of threatened loss of prospective customers and goodwill certainly supports a finding
27   of irreparable harm.” Stuhlbarg Int’l Sales Co. v. John D. Brush & Co., 240 F.3d 832, 841 (9th Cir.
28   2001).

1           Disruption of User Relationships and Subscription Continuity. Ex-Human built its iOS

2    user base over nearly four years, including more than 2.3 million installs of Botify. Compl. ¶ 34.
3    Following Apple’s actions, Ex-Human has lost the ability to serve those users through iOS, acquire

4    new iOS users, or continue subscription billing through the App Store. Rodichev Decl. ¶ 38. Users

5    have already contacted Ex-Human regarding the unavailability of its applications and the inability

6    to continue using or purchasing services. Rodichev Decl. ¶ 39.

7           Compounding Loss of Goodwill and Market Position. Each day that Ex-Human remains

8    excluded from the App Store further disrupts user relationships, increases attrition, and diminishes
9    the likelihood that users will return even if access is later restored. Rodichev Decl. ¶ 51. In

10   consumer software markets, lost user engagement and momentum are difficult or impossible to

11   recreate after the fact. These harms are not readily quantifiable and cannot be fully remedied

12   through damages. See Rent-A-Ctr., Inc. v. Canyon Television & Appliance Rental, Inc., 944 F.2d

13   597, 603 (9th Cir. 1991) (“intangible injuries, such as damage to ongoing recruitment efforts and

14   goodwill, qualify as irreparable harm”).
15          Loss of Ability to Compete in the iOS Ecosystem. Apple’s actions have eliminated Ex-

16   Human’s ability to compete within the iOS ecosystem. The removal of Photify and Botify from the

17   App Store prevents Ex-Human from reaching iOS users entirely. Compl. ¶ 66. The threat of being
18   driven out of a market supports a finding of irreparable harm. Am. Passage Media Corp. v. Cass

19   Commc’ns, Inc., 750 F.2d 1470, 1474 (9th Cir. 1985) (“[t]he threat of being driven out of business

20   is sufficient to establish irreparable harm”); Douglas Dynamics, LLC v. Buyers Prod. Co., 717 F.3d

21   1336, 1345 (Fed. Cir. 2013) (“mere damages will not compensate for a competitor's increasing

22   share of the market”).

23          Imminent Shutdown. Apple’s conduct is causing immediate and existential harm to Ex-
24   Human’s business. Before Apple’s actions, iOS was Ex-Human’s primary revenue channel,

4    revenue and release of withheld funds, will likely need to reduce at least half of its remaining

5    workforce within the next 30 days. Id. at ¶ 46. If that occurs, Ex-Human will be forced to suspend

6    most product development and operate only at a minimum maintenance level, placing the company

7    on a path toward shutdown. Id. These harms—including loss of employees, operational capacity,

8    and the ability to continue as a going concern—are irreparable because they cannot be fully
9    remedied after the fact. See hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 273 F. Supp. 3d 1099, 1105-06 (N.D.

10   Cal. 2017).

11          No Adequate Substitute for Lost App Store Distribution. Ex-Human’s existing web version

12   does not mitigate the irreparable harm caused by Apple’s actions. Rodichev Decl. ¶¶ 48-49. The

13   web version has historically generated significantly less revenue and does not restore App Store

14   discovery, native iOS distribution, subscription continuity, retention, or overall revenue
15   performance. Id. Existing iOS subscribers also cannot readily be migrated from Apple’s billing

16   system to web billing. Id. Nor can Ex-Human offset these losses through other platforms: as

17   demonstrated in the record, Apple’s actions have also caused a decline in Google Play revenue by
18   forcing Ex-Human to reduce marketing and user-acquisition efforts across the business. Id. at

19   ¶¶ 41-42. Web and Android channels therefore do not provide an adequate substitute for the lost

20   iOS business and do not mitigate the irreparable harm resulting from Apple’s conduct.

21          No Adequate Remedy at Law. Courts have recognized that exclusion from a platform on

22   which a business depends, where no viable alternative exists, constitutes irreparable harm. See hiQ

23   Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 31 F.4th 1180, 1189 (9th Cir. 2022) (affirming preliminary injunction
24   where plaintiff's business relied on access to LinkedIn profiles and there was “no current viable

25   alternative”). That is the situation here. Without interim relief, Ex-Human remains entirely

26   excluded from the iOS platform, and the resulting harm to its business, user relationships, goodwill

27   will continue to compound. Compl. ¶ 66.

28

1    II.    INTERIM RELIEF PRESERVES THE STATUS QUO AND THE BALANCE OF
            EQUITIES FAVORS RELIEF
2
3           Apple, by contrast, will suffer no cognizable harm from restoration of the status quo. The

4    status quo is defined as “the last actual peaceable, uncontested status which preceded the pending

5    controversy.” 14859 Moorpark Homeowner's Ass'n v. VRT Corp., 63 Cal. App. 4th 1396, 1408

6    (1998). The relief sought here would return the parties to the pre-January 24, 2026 state, when Ex-

7    Human maintained an active developer account, its applications remained available on the App

8    Store, and it was able to serve its iOS user base.

9           Reinstatement would preserve that status quo and halt the ongoing disruption to Ex-

10   Human’s iOS business pending adjudication on the merits. Without interim relief, Ex-Human

11   remains excluded from the only channel through which it can reach iOS users, and the resulting

12   harm continues to compound. Compl. ¶ 66.

13          Apple has identified no specific harm—financial, operational, or otherwise—that would

14   result from temporarily restoring Ex-Human’s developer account. Id. at ¶¶ 45, 47-48, 50, 54. In its

15   termination communications, Apple repeatedly invoked generalized allegations of misconduct but

16   did not identify any specific conduct or resulting risk associated with Ex-Human’s continued

17   participation in the Developer Program. Id. Where a platform operator has permitted a business to

18   operate for years without identifying concrete harm, courts have found no cognizable injury from

19   temporary continued access pending adjudication. See hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 273 F.

20   Supp. 3d 1099, 1107 (N.D. Cal. 2017).

21          By contrast, absent reinstatement, Ex-Human faces ongoing and irreparable harm from its

22   exclusion from the iOS platform, including disruption of user relationships, loss of goodwill, loss

23   of its primary revenue channel, and a decline in revenue across other platforms caused by forced

24   reductions in marketing and user acquisition. Apple’s continued withholding of approximately

25   $506,000 in earned proceeds further exacerbates Ex-Human’s liquidity crisis, leading to imminent

26   financial harm, additional layoffs, and a likely operational shutdown. Rodichev Decl. ¶¶ 31, 40-46,

27   56. The balance of equities therefore strongly favors interim relief. Compl. ¶ 66.

28

1    III.   EX-HUMAN IS LIKELY TO SUCCEED, OR AT MINIMUM RAISES SERIOUS
            QUESTIONS, BECAUSE APPLE CONTINUES TO ENFORCE TERMINATION
2           BASED ON UNIDENTIFIED MISCONDUCT
3           “[W]hen plaintiffs establish that the balance of hardships tips sharply in their favor, there is

4    a likelihood of irreparable injury, and the injunction is in the public interest, they need only show

5    ‘serious questions’ on the merits.” Where Do We Go Berkeley v. California Dep't of Transp., 32

6    F.4th 852, 859 (9th Cir. 2022). As demonstrated above, Ex-Human has established the first three

7    factors. At a minimum, Ex-Human raises serious questions going to the merits of whether Apple

8    may continue to enforce termination and withhold revenue on a misconduct-based rationale without

9    identifying the conduct it contends violated the DPLA.

10          A.      Apple Invoked Misconduct-Based Provisions Without Identifying the
                    Conduct It Contends Violated Them
11

12          Apple invoked Section 3.2(f) of the DPLA and related App Review Guidelines as the basis

13   for removing Ex-Human’s applications and terminating its developer account. Compl. ¶¶ 42, 45,

14   47-48, 50, 54. Across multiple notices and appeal responses, Apple repeatedly asserted “dishonest

15   or fraudulent activity” and other forms of misconduct. Id.

16          At no point, however, did Apple identify any specific submission, transaction, content item,

17   or other act that it contends violated those provisions. Id. Nor did Apple identify any specific

18   instance of the alleged misconduct despite having full visibility into Ex-Human’s applications and

19   transaction data. Id. at ¶ 57. Instead, Apple relied on generalized descriptions of possible violations

20   while continuing to impose the most severe consequence available to it—complete exclusion from

21   the iOS platform. Id. at ¶¶ 45, 47-48, 50, 54. Apple’s continued enforcement of termination on that

22   basis—without identifying the conduct it contends triggered Section 3.2(f)—raises serious

23   questions as to whether it is acting within the bounds of its contractual discretion.

24          B.      That Conduct Likely Breaches the Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair
                    Dealing
25

26          California law implies a covenant of good faith and fair dealing in every contract. Guz v.

27   Bechtel Nat. Inc., 24 Cal. 4th 317, 349, 8 P.3d 1089, 1110 (2000). The covenant prevents a party

28   from exercising contractual discretion in a manner that unfairly frustrates the agreed purposes of
                                         10
                          MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
      Case 3:26-cv-02798-JD           Document 23       Filed 04/22/26      Page 15 of 19



1    the contract or deprives the other party of its benefits. Carma Developers, Inc. v. Marathon Dev.

2    Cal., Inc., 2 Cal. 4th 342, 372 (1992). Apple exercised its discretion to terminate Ex-Human’s
3    developer account and remove its applications based on alleged misconduct, while refusing to

4    identify the conduct underlying that determination. Compl. ¶¶ 45, 47-48, 50, 54. Throughout its

5    communications, Apple asserted “dishonest or fraudulent activity” but did not identify any specific

6    submission, transaction, content item, or act supporting that conclusion. Id.

7           That absence of specificity is particularly significant given Apple’s access to

8    comprehensive application and transaction data. Apple possessed full visibility into Ex-Human’s
9    applications and operations, yet identified no concrete instance of the misconduct it cited. Compl.

10   ¶¶ 45, 47-48, 50, 54, 57. A decision to impose the most severe consequence available—termination

11   and complete exclusion from the platform—without identifying any specific underlying conduct

12   raises serious questions as to whether Apple engaged in an individualized, good-faith

13   determination. See In re Bank of America California Unemployment Benefits Litig., 674 F. Supp.

14   3d 884, 901 (S.D. Cal. 2023).
15          Ex-Human repeatedly attempted to engage with Apple, provide information about its

16   applications, and implement any safeguards. Id. at ¶¶ 44, 46, 49, 52-53. Apple nevertheless

17   continued to rely on generalized allegations while enforcing termination. At a minimum, this course
18   of conduct raises serious questions as to whether Apple exercised its contractual discretion

19   consistent with the implied covenant.

20          Ex-Human also alleges facts supporting an inference that Apple’s actions were not the result

21   of a neutral, individualized determination. Apple removed Photify, an application with

22   functionality overlapping Apple’s own Image Playground, while continuing to assert generalized

23   misconduct without identifying specific conduct. Id. at ¶¶ 10-13, 45, 47-48, 50, 54, 57. These facts
24   further support the conclusion that Apple’s exercise of discretion raises serious questions under the

25   implied covenant.

26          Apple’s withholding of earned revenue without identifying any transaction-level basis

27   further supports that inference. Apple has not identified any specific fraudulent transaction, refund

28   obligation, or other concrete basis for withholding approximately $500,000 in earned proceeds. Id.
                                         11
                          MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
      Case 3:26-cv-02798-JD          Document 23         Filed 04/22/26      Page 16 of 19



1    at ¶ 57. The continued withholding of earned revenue without identified basis raises additional

2    questions as to whether Apple’s conduct was consistent with its contractual obligations.
3           C.      Apple’s Conduct Likely Violates California’s Unfair Competition Law, Cal.
                    Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200
4

5           California’s Unfair Competition Law prohibits any “unlawful, unfair or fraudulent business

6    act or practice.” Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200. At a minimum, Ex-Human raises serious questions

7    going to the merits of its UCL claim because Apple’s conduct, as alleged, is unfair within the

8    meaning of Section 17200. The same course of conduct that supports Ex-Human’s contract-based
9    claims also supports equitable relief under the UCL.

10          Apple repeatedly asserted that Ex-Human engaged in “dishonest or fraudulent activity” and

11   later cited App Review Guidelines 1.1, 1.1.4, and 5.6, yet it did not identify any specific submission,

12   transaction, content item, or other act that it contends violated those provisions. Compl. ¶¶ 42-54.

13   Apple nevertheless continued to enforce Ex-Human’s exclusion from the App Store and to withhold

14   approximately $500,000 in earned developer proceeds without identifying any specific refund
15   obligation, chargeback, or transaction-level basis for doing so. Compl. ¶¶ 55-61. On these

16   allegations, Ex-Human has at minimum raised serious questions as to whether Apple’s exercise of

17   its gatekeeper authority—terminating a developer, excluding its applications, and withholding
18   substantial earned proceeds while refusing to identify any underlying conduct or transaction-level

19   basis—constitutes an unfair business practice within the meaning of the UCL. Epic Games, Inc. v.

20   Apple, Inc., 67 F.4th 946, 1000-01 (9th Cir. 2023) (reasoning that “[t]he unfair prong is

21   intentionally framed in its broad, sweeping language, precisely to enable judicial tribunals to deal

22   with the innumerable new schemes which the fertility of man’s invention would contrive”) (internal

23   quotation marks omitted).
24          Apple controls the only authorized distribution channel for native iOS applications in the

25   United States. Id. at ¶ 66. At the same time, Apple offers its own competing AI image-generation

26   application, Image Playground, which Ex-Human alleges overlaps substantially with Photify in

27   core functionality and user flow. Id. at ¶¶ 36–40. Apple removed Photify from the App Store while

28   continuing to offer Image Playground on the same platform, all while refusing to identify the
                                         12
                          MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
      Case 3:26-cv-02798-JD           Document 23       Filed 04/22/26     Page 17 of 19



1    specific conduct it contends justified its misconduct determination. Id. In those circumstances, Ex-

2    Human has at minimum raised serious questions whether Apple’s opaque exercise of platform
3    power to exclude a competing application and withhold earned proceeds is unfair within the

4    meaning of Section 17200. hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 273 F. Supp. 3d 1099, 1117-18 (N.D.

5    Cal. 2017) (finding serious questions on UCL unfairness claim where platform operator plausibly

6    used its control over essential data access to cut off a rival while developing a competing product

7    and thereby leveraged dominance to gain a competitive advantage).

8           Apple’s conduct has caused Ex-Human to lose money and property in the form of withheld
9    developer proceeds, lost App Store distribution, lost user relationships, lost goodwill, and lost

10   revenue associated with the removal of Botify and Photify from the App Store. Compl. ¶¶ 55-66,

11   110-117. Those allegations are sufficient to support UCL standing and further support interim

12   equitable relief pending adjudication on the merits.
13          D.      Apple’s Withholding of Earned Proceeds Without Identified Basis Further
                    Supports Serious Questions on the Merits
14
15          Ex-Human’s breach of contract claim regarding withheld revenue is straightforward.

16   Schedule 2, Section 7.1 of the DPLA permits Apple to withhold developer earnings in limited

17   circumstances, including to account for refunds or where Apple determines or suspects misconduct.
18   Id. at ¶ 27. Apple has not identified any specific transaction subject to a refund obligation. Id. at

19   ¶ 57. It has not articulated any transaction-level basis for its suspicion of misconduct. It has

20   provided no accounting of how the withheld funds are being held or applied. Id. at ¶ 58. Apple

21   continues to withhold approximately $500,000 in earned developer proceeds from completed

22   transactions without identifying any refund basis, suspected misconduct, or other specific

23   contractual justification. Id. at ¶¶ 55-58.
24          Even where contractual language grants discretion, that discretion must be exercised in a

25   manner consistent with the contract. In Free Range Content, Inc. v. Google Inc., No. 14-CV-02329-

26   BLF, 2016 WL 2902332 (N.D. Cal. May 13, 2016), the court held that Google could not rely on

27   broad discretionary language to justify withholding payments without actually exercising that

28   discretion in a grounded and specific manner. Apple’s position here is weaker: it has not identified
                                         13
                          MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES
      Case 3:26-cv-02798-JD             Document 23         Filed 04/22/26      Page 18 of 19



1    any transaction, refund, or specific basis for withholding the funds at issue. This conduct

2    independently raises serious questions on the merits.
3    IV.        THE PUBLIC INTEREST SUPPORTS INTERIM RELIEF
4               The public interest favors interim relief. Botify served a substantial iOS user base before its
5    removal, and Apple’s termination of Ex-Human’s developer account has disrupted access for users
6    who relied on Ex-Human’s applications through the App Store. Compl. ¶ 54. Preserving access to
7    an operating consumer service pending adjudication serves the public interest, particularly where
8    the platform operator has not identified the specific conduct it contends justified termination. See
9    hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 31 F.4th 1180, 1202 (9th Cir. 2022) (public interest favored
10   preliminary relief preserving continued access to a publicly available platform pending
11   adjudication).
12              The public interest also favors fair and transparent enforcement of platform rules. Ex-
13   Human does not seek to prevent Apple from enforcing its agreements or policies. It seeks only
14   interim relief where Apple invoked misconduct-based provisions, terminated Ex-Human’s account,
15   and continues to enforce that termination without identifying the conduct it contends violated those
16   provisions. Temporary reinstatement pending further proceedings therefore serves the public
17   interest by preserving user access and ensuring that serious misconduct allegations are enforced in
18   a manner consistent with the parties’ agreements.
19         V.      CONCLUSION
20              For the foregoing reasons, Ex-Human respectfully requests that the Court enter a temporary
21   restraining order restoring Ex-Human’s Apple Developer Program membership and reinstating its
22   applications to the App Store pending further proceedings. Apple invoked misconduct-based
23   provisions to terminate Ex-Human’s account, yet never identified the conduct it contends justified
24   that determination, while Ex-Human continues to suffer immediate and irreparable harm from
25   exclusion from the iOS platform. That harm includes the loss of Ex-Human’s primary revenue
26   channel, the continued withholding of approximately $506,000 in earned proceeds, and resulting
27   severe financial distress, including imminent further layoffs and a likely operational shutdown
28   absent relief. Interim relief is necessary to preserve the status quo and prevent that harm from
